text: Unit 1 – Introduction & Computer System Organization

subject: UNKNOWN
text: Operating Systems (OS) form the backbone of modern computing systems. Every application program, from a simple calculator to complex AI software, relies on the operating system to interact with the hardware. Without an operating system, application developers would need to write hardware-specific code, making software development extremely complex and impractical.

subject: UNKNOWN
text: If an operating system were not developed, application developers would need to directly interact with hardware components such as the CPU, memory, disk, and I/O devices. This would require detailed knowledge of hardware architecture, device protocols, and low-level instructions. The operating system abstracts hardware complexity and provides a standardized interface, allowing developers to focus on solving problems rather than managing hardware.

subject: UNKNOWN
heading_path: General Definition of an Operating System
text: An Operating System is a program that acts as an intermediary between the user and the computer hardware. It provides a user-friendly environment in which users can easily develop and execute programs. Without an operating system: • Hardware knowledge would be mandatory for programming • Software portability would be extremely limited • Resource conflicts would be difficult to manage

subject: UNKNOWN
text: Early computers did not have operating systems. Programs were loaded manually, and only one program could run at a time. Over time, as hardware became more powerful and users demanded multitasking, operating systems evolved to manage resources efficiently and provide better usability.

text: Pavan A C (pavanac@pes.edu) 2 Operating System Goals The primary goals of an operating system are: • Execute user programs and make solving user problems easier • Make the computer system convenient to use • Use hardware efficiently • Manage system resources, including: o Memory o Processor(s) o Input/Output devices An effective OS balances user convenience with efficient hardware utilization. Why Study Operating Systems? Although only a small percentage of computer professionals design or modify operating systems, almost all software runs on top of an OS. Understanding operating systems is crucial for: • Writing efficient programs • Developing secure applications

subject: UNKNOWN
text: • Debugging performance issues • Understanding resource behavior such as memory usage and CPU scheduling Knowledge of OS fundamentals leads to proper, efficient, effective, and secure programming. Four Components of a Computer System (Abstract View) A computer system can be divided into four major components: 1. Hardware - Provides basic computing resources such as: o CPU o Main memory

Application Programs - Define how system resources are used to solve user problems Examples: o Word processors o Compilers o Web browsers o Database systems o Video games 4. Users - Can be people, machines, or other computers.

subject: UNKNOWN
text: The operating system sits between hardware and application programs, ensuring safe and efficient usage of system resources. What Operating Systems Do (User vs System View) From the user’s perspective: • Desire convenience • Want ease of use • Expect good performance • Do not care much about resource utilization From the system’s perspective: • Especially in shared systems (mainframes, minicomputers) • Must ensure fair resource allocation • Must maximize utilization of: o CPU time o Memory o I/O devices • No single user should monopolize resources What Operating Systems Do (Different Environments) • Dedicated systems (workstations): Have dedicated resources but

text: still rely on shared servers (file, print, compute servers) • Handheld devices: Resource-constrained, optimized for: o Battery life o Usability

System View of Operating System From a system viewpoint, the operating system serves two major roles: 1. Resource Allocator o Manages all system resources o Resolves conflicting resource requests o Ensures fairness and efficiency 2. Control Program o Controls execution of programs o Prevents errors o Prevents improper use of the computer Defining the Operating System The fundamental goal of a

text: An operating system is interrupt-driven. • Interrupt transfers control to an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) • Uses an interrupt vector containing addresses of service routines • CPU state (program counter, registers) is saved A trap or exception is a software-generated interrupt caused by: • Errors • User requests (system calls)

text: Steps in interrupt handling: 1. Save current CPU state 2. Identify interrupt type 3. Execute appropriate interrupt service routine 4. Restore CPU state 5. Resume execution Interrupt identification methods: • Polling • Vectored interrupt systems
